title: Law of Radioactive Decay
subtitle: Rutherford & Soddy (1902) fundamental differential equation
contentHtml:
The rate of decay of a radioactive parent isotope is strictly proportional to the number of radioactive atoms present at that instant:

- dN / dt = λ · N

Integrating from $t = 0$ ($N_0$ parent atoms) to time $t$ yields the exponential decay law:

N(t) = N₀ · e^(-λt)
  • Decay Constant (λ): Probability of an individual nucleus decaying per unit time ($ ext{yr}^{-1}$ or $ ext{s}^{-1}$). Independent of temperature, pressure, or chemical bonding.
  • Accumulated Radiogenic Daughter (D*): $D^* = N_0 - N = N cdot (e^{lambda t} - 1)$.
deepDive:
Total Daughter Equation:

  • In nature, a rock typically starts with some initial non-radiogenic daughter atoms ($D_0$) inherited at crystallization:
  • $D_ ext{total} = D_0 + N(t) cdot (e^{lambda t} - 1)$.
  • For small $lambda t ll 1$ (e.g. young rocks or long half-lives), $e^{lambda t} - 1 approx lambda t$, simplifying to $D^* approx N lambda t$.
eli5: Think of an hourglass where sand grains drop at a fixed statistical rate. If you count how many grains have fallen into the bottom (daughter) versus how many are still on top (parent), you know exactly how long the hourglass has been running!

title: Half-Life (t₁/₂) & Mean Life (τ) Interconversions
subtitle: Mathematical relationships tested in geochronology numericals
contentHtml:
The time required for half of the initial radioactive parent atoms to decay is the Half-Life ($t_{1/2}$):

N / N₀ = 1/2 = e^(-λ · t₁/₂)  ⟹  t₁/₂ = ln(2) / λ ≈ 0.69315 / λ

The Mean Life ($ au$) is the average lifetime of a radioactive nucleus before decaying:

τ = 1 / λ = t₁/₂ / ln(2) ≈ 1.4427 · t₁/₂

quiz.question: If a radioactive parent isotope has a decay constant λ = 1.42 × 10⁻¹¹ yr⁻¹ (such as ⁸⁷Rb), what is its corresponding half-life (t₁/₂)?
options: 4.88 × 10¹⁰ years (48.8 Ga)
7.04 × 10⁸ years (704 Ma)
quiz.rationale: t₁/₂ = ln(2) / λ = 0.693147 / (1.42 × 10⁻¹¹ yr⁻¹) ≈ 4.881 × 10¹⁰ years = 48.8 Ga (billion years).

deepDive:
Half-Life Milestones:

  • After 1 half-life: 50% parent remains, D/N = 1.
  • After 2 half-lives: 25% parent remains, D/N = 3.
  • After 3 half-lives: 12.5% parent remains, D/N = 7.
  • After $n$ half-lives: $N/N_0 = (1/2)^n$, and $D^*/N = 2^n - 1$.
eli5: After one half-life, half your candy is gone. After two half-lives, three quarters are gone. By measuring the ratio of eaten candy (daughter) to remaining candy (parent), you can calculate the exact time elapsed.

title: Secular vs Transient Radioactive Equilibrium
subtitle: Decay chains and intermediate daughter accumulation regimes
contentHtml:
In a decay chain ($P longrightarrow D_1 longrightarrow D_2$), equilibrium occurs when the daughter's rate of production equals its rate of decay:

Equilibrium TypeConditionActivity RelationshipGeological Example
Secular Equilibrium $lambda_1 ll lambda_2$ ($t_{1/2}^ ext{parent} ggg t_{1/2}^ ext{daughter}$) $A_1 = A_2 implies lambda_1 N_1 = lambda_2 N_2$ $^{238}U ightarrow {}^{234}Th ightarrow {}^{230}Th$ in undisturbed ancient rocks (>1 Ma)
Transient Equilibrium $lambda_1 < lambda_2$ ($t_{1/2}^ ext{parent} > t_{1/2}^ ext{daughter}$, but comparable) $N_2 / N_1 = lambda_1 / (lambda_2 - lambda_1)$ $^{232}Th ightarrow {}^{228}Ra$
No Equilibrium $lambda_1 > lambda_2$ (Parent decays faster than daughter) Daughter accumulates and outlives parent Extinct radionuclides: $^{26}Al ightarrow {}^{26}Mg$, $^{182}Hf ightarrow {}^{182}W$
deepDive:
U-Series Disequilibrium Dating:

  • In oceans and weathering zones, chemical fractionation separates uranium ($U^{6+}$, soluble) from thorium ($Th^{4+}$, insoluble).
  • This breaks secular equilibrium, creating $(^{230}Th/^{238}U)$ disequilibrium, which serves as a high-precision chronometer for speleothems, corals, and young volcanic eruptions (<350 ka).
eli5: Secular equilibrium is like a leaky bucket (daughter) filled by a giant lake (parent). Water drains out of the bucket at the exact same rate it pours in from the lake, keeping the bucket's water level perfectly steady!

title: The Isochron Principle: Eliminating Initial Daughter
subtitle: Why we normalize by a stable, non-radiogenic isotope
contentHtml:
The basic daughter accumulation equation contains two unknowns: age ($t$) and initial daughter ($D_0$):

D = D₀ + P · (e^(λt) - 1)

To eliminate reliance on guessing $D_0$, we divide all terms by a stable, non-radiogenic reference isotope of the daughter element ($D_ ext{stable}$):

(D / D_stable) = (D₀ / D_stable) + (P / D_stable) · (e^(λt) - 1)

This forms the linear equation $y = c + m cdot x$ of a straight line: the Isochron.

quiz.question: What are the two fundamental assumptions required for a collection of cogenetic rock or mineral samples to yield a valid radiometric isochron?
options: Samples must have identical parent/daughter concentrations and zero radioactive decay
All samples formed at the exact same time (t), had identical initial isotopic ratios (D₀/D_stable), and remained closed systems to chemical exchange
Samples must have been heated above 1000 °C continuously until the present day
The half-life of the parent isotope must vary directly with sample depth
quiz.rationale: An isochron requires that all sub-samples: (1) are co-genetic (formed at the same time t), (2) were isotopically homogeneous at t = 0 (same initial ratio D₀/D_ref), and (3) remained strictly closed systems without loss or gain of parent or daughter.

deepDive:
Isochron Variables Mapping:

  • y: Measured daughter ratio $(D/D_ ext{ref})$.
  • x: Measured parent/daughter ratio $(P/D_ ext{ref})$.
  • Slope ($m$): $e^{lambda t} - 1 approx lambda t$ $implies$ gives the Age ($t$).
  • y-intercept ($c$): Initial ratio $(D/D_ ext{ref})_0$ $implies$ gives the Source Reservoir!
eli5: You can't know how much daughter was already in the rock at birth just by looking at one mineral. But by testing several minerals from the same rock, they all line up on a straight line. The steepness of the line tells you the age, and where it hits the wall tells you the starting baby formula!

title: The Rb-Sr Decay Scheme & Physics
subtitle: Beta-minus decay of Rubidium-87 into Strontium-87
contentHtml:
Rubidium-87 ($^{87}_{37}Rb$) decays to Strontium-87 ($^{87}_{38}Sr$) via beta-minus ($ eta^-$) emission:

⁸⁷₃₇Rb ⟶ ⁸⁷₃₈Sr + β⁻ + ν̄_e + Q (0.282 MeV)
  • Neutron Conversion: Inside the nucleus: $n longrightarrow p + e^- + ar{ u}_e$. Mass number $A = 87$ remains constant (isobaric transition).
  • Decay Constant: $lambda = 1.42 imes 10^{-11} ext{ yr}^{-1}$ (IUGS Steiger & Jäger convention, 1977).
  • Half-Life: $t_{1/2} = 4.88 imes 10^{10} ext{ years (48.8 Ga)}$. (Some recent revisions suggest $lambda = 1.393 imes 10^{-11} ext{ yr}^{-1}, t_{1/2} = 49.7 ext{ Ga}$).
  • Natural Abundance: $^{87}Rb$ constitutes 27.83% of natural rubidium ($^{85}Rb = 72.17%$).
deepDive:
Strontium Stable Isotopes:

  • Natural Strontium has 4 stable isotopes:
    • $^{88}Sr$: 82.58% (most abundant)
    • $^{87}Sr$: ~7.00% (variable due to radiogenic growth from $^{87}Rb$)
    • $^{86}Sr$: 9.86% (non-radiogenic reference isotope)
    • $^{84}Sr$: 0.56%
  • Standardization: Mass spectrometer instrumental fractionation is normalized to constant $^{86}Sr/^{88}Sr = 0.1194$.
eli5: Rubidium-87 is an unstable atom that fires off a tiny electron (beta particle) to turn into stable Strontium-87. It does this at a super-slow speed, taking nearly 49 billion years for half of it to decay!

subtitle: Ionic radius, valence, and mineral substitution rules
contentHtml:
The geochemical contrast between Rb and Sr drives their separation during igneous crystallization:

quiz.question: Which of the following mineral pairs represents an ideal pairing of HIGH Rb/Sr and LOW Rb/Sr minerals from the same granitic rock for constructng an internal mineral isochron?
options: Quartz (high Rb/Sr) and Zircon (low Rb/Sr)
Biotite (high Rb/Sr) and Plagioclase (low Rb/Sr)
Olivine (high Rb/Sr) and Clinopyroxene (low Rb/Sr)
Magnetite (high Rb/Sr) and Ilmenite (low Rb/Sr)
quiz.rationale: Biotite readily incorporates K⁺ and therefore Rb⁺, but rejects Sr²⁺ (extremely high Rb/Sr ratio). Plagioclase incorporates Ca²⁺ and therefore Sr²⁺, but excludes Rb⁺ (extremely low Rb/Sr ratio). This produces the maximum spread in x-axis values necessary for an accurate isochron!

deepDive:
Typical Mineral Rb/Sr Ratios:

  • Biotite: $^{87}Rb/^{86}Sr approx 10 ext{ to }>100$ (steep radiogenic growth).
  • Muscovite: $^{87}Rb/^{86}Sr approx 5 ext{ to }30$.
  • K-feldspar: $^{87}Rb/^{86}Sr approx 1 ext{ to }5$.
  • Plagioclase: $^{87}Rb/^{86}Sr approx 0.01 ext{ to }0.2$ (anchors the y-intercept $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)_0$).
  • Apatite: $^{87}Rb/^{86}Sr approx 0.001$ (nearly pure initial strontium).
eli5: Rb mimics Potassium (K) and loves hiding in dark biotite mica flakes. Sr mimics Calcium (Ca) and loves white plagioclase crystals. Because they separate so cleanly, they give geologists the perfect contrast to measure time!

title: The Rb-Sr Isochron Equation
subtitle: Complete mathematical formula and graphical anatomy
contentHtml:
The working whole-rock and mineral Rb-Sr isochron equation is:

(⁸⁷Sr / ⁸⁶Sr)_present = (⁸⁷Sr / ⁸⁶Sr)₀ + (⁸⁷Rb / ⁸⁶Sr) · (e^(λt) - 1)

Plotting $y = (^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)$ against $x = (^{87}Rb/^{86}Sr)$ gives:

  • Slope ($m$): $m = e^{lambda t} - 1 approx lambda t$ (for $lambda t ll 1$).
    Solving for age: $mathbf{t = rac{1}{lambda} ln(m + 1) approx rac{m}{lambda}}$.
  • Y-Intercept ($c$): Initial Strontium ratio $mathbf{(^{87}Sr / ^{86}Sr)_0}$ inherited at the time of magma crystallization ($t = 0$).
  • Clock Hand Analogy: At $t = 0$, all co-genetic samples lie on a horizontal line ($m = 0$). As time ticks, the line rotates counterclockwise around the pivot point $(0, c)$.
deepDive:
How to Measure Rb/Sr in the Lab:

  • $^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr$ ratio is measured with ultra-high precision using Thermal Ionization Mass Spectrometry (TIMS) or MC-ICP-MS.
  • Total $Rb$ and $Sr$ concentrations (ppm) are determined via Isotope Dilution (ID) or X-ray Fluorescence (XRF).
  • Atomic conversion: $^{87}Rb/^{86}Sr = (Rb/Sr)_ ext{ppm} imes rac{0.2783 imes 87.62}{85.4678 imes 0.0986} approx 2.893 imes (Rb/Sr)_ ext{wt}$.
eli5: At day zero, all minerals in a cooled magma have the exact same Sr isotope ratio—forming a flat horizontal line. Over billions of years, minerals with lots of Rb produce extra radiogenic ⁸⁷Sr, tilting the line up. The steeper the tilt, the older the rock!

title: Numerical Problem: Rb-Sr Rock Age
subtitle: Direct GATE exam numerical computation from isochron slope
contentHtml:
A suite of cogenetic granitic rocks yields a linear Rb-Sr whole-rock isochron:

(⁸⁷Sr / ⁸⁶Sr) = 0.7040 + 0.0355 · (⁸⁷Rb / ⁸⁶Sr)

Given the decay constant of Rubidium-87 is $lambda = 1.42 imes 10^{-11} ext{ yr}^{-1}$.

quiz.question: What is the crystallization age of this granitic suite?
options: 500 Ma

deepDive:
Intercept Interpretation:

  • The y-intercept is $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)_0 = 0.7040$.
  • This low initial ratio indicates a juvenile magma derived directly from a slightly depleted mantle or short-lived mafic crust, with minimal contamination from ancient continental crust!
eli5: Take the slope (0.0355) and divide it by the decay constant (1.42 × 10⁻¹¹). In seconds, you discover the granite formed exactly 2.5 billion years ago during the Archean Eon!

title: Initial (⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr)₀: Magma Source Fingerprint
subtitle: Distinguishing mantle-derived I-type vs crustal S-type granites
contentHtml:
Because mantle and continental crust have vastly different $Rb/Sr$ ratios, the initial Strontium ratio $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)_0$ reveals the petrogenetic source of magma:

Initial Ratio $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)_0$Magma SourceRock Association / Granite Type
0.7020 – 0.7035 Depleted Upper Mantle Mid-Ocean Ridge Basalts (MORBs), Ophiolites
0.7040 – 0.7060 Undepleted / Enriched Mantle or Island Arcs Ocean Island Basalts (OIBs), I-type (igneous) Granitoids
0.7060 – 0.7100 Mixed Source / Crustal Contamination Continental flood basalts with crustal assimilation
> 0.7100 (up to 0.730+) Ancient Continental Crust (Sialic basement) S-type (sedimentary anatectic) Granites, Pegmatites
deepDive:
Why Ancient Crust Has High Sr Ratios:

  • Continental crust was extracted with high $Rb/Sr$ billions of years ago. Over 2 to 3 billion years, decay of abundant $^{87}Rb$ has pushed its $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)$ up to 0.715–0.740.
  • When continental rocks melt (e.g. Himalayan leucogranites), the resulting granites inherit this high ratio directly!
eli5: The initial Sr ratio is like a genetic passport: A low number (~0.703) means the magma was born pure from the deep mantle. A high number (>0.710) proves it is melted ancient continental crust!

title: Granite Petrogenesis from Initial ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr
subtitle: Diagnostic GATE question on I-type vs S-type granites
contentHtml:
Two granitic plutons, Pluton Alpha and Pluton Beta, were emplaced at 500 Ma during an orogenic event:

  • Pluton Alpha: Isochron y-intercept $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)_0 = 0.7042$, contains hornblende and sphene.
  • Pluton Beta: Isochron y-intercept $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)_0 = 0.7185$, contains muscovite, cordierite, and tourmaline.

quiz.question: Based on their mineralogy and initial ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr ratios, which classification and petrogenetic origin correctly describes these two plutons?
options: Both Alpha and Beta are mantle-derived peralkaline granites
Pluton Alpha is an I-type granite derived from mantle/juvenile crust; Pluton Beta is an S-type granite derived from melting of ancient pelitic metasediments
Pluton Alpha is an S-type granite; Pluton Beta is an I-type granite
Pluton Beta formed by direct fractional crystallization of depleted MORB magma
quiz.rationale: Pluton Alpha has a low initial ratio (0.7042) and metaluminous hornblende/sphene, diagnostic of I-type (igneous precursor) granites. Pluton Beta has a very high initial ratio (0.7185) and peraluminous minerals (muscovite, cordierite, tourmaline), characteristic of S-type granites formed by anatexis of clay-rich sedimentary crust.

deepDive:
Chappell & White (1974) Criteria:

  • I-type: Metaluminous to mildly peraluminous ($ASI < 1.1$), $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)_0 < 0.706$, hornblende, titanite, magnetite.
  • S-type: Strongly peraluminous ($ASI > 1.1$), $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)_0 > 0.708$, muscovite, garnet, cordierite, ilmenite.
eli5: Alpha's low Sr ratio (0.704) and hornblende tell you it came from melted igneous rocks or the mantle (I-type). Beta's sky-high Sr ratio (0.718) and muscovite prove it came from baked mudstone and clay sediments (S-type)!

title: BABI & Earth's Strontium Evolution Curve
subtitle: Basaltic Achondrite Best Initial and primordial solar strontium
contentHtml:
To understand strontium isotope evolution, geochemists define primeval solar benchmarks:

  • BABI (Basaltic Achondrite Best Initial): $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr) = mathbf{0.69897 pm 0.00003}$. Determined from calcium-rich achondrite meteorites (eclogites/eucrites) with essentially zero Rb. Represents the initial ratio of the solar system at $t = 4.567 ext{ Ga}$.
  • ALL (Allende CAI Initial): Even lower: $mathbf{0.69877}$.
  • Bulk Silicate Earth (BSE) Today: Starting from BABI at 4.567 Ga with $(Rb/Sr)_ ext{BSE} approx 0.089$, Earth's undifferentiated mantle has evolved to $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)_ ext{UR} approx mathbf{0.7045}$ today.
deepDive:
Evolution Divergence:

  • During early crust formation (~4.0–2.5 Ga), continental crust stripped Rb, driving its ratio upward (>0.710).
  • The residual depleted mantle was left starved of Rb ($Rb/Sr approx 0.02$), evolving very sluggishly to only ~0.7025 today!
eli5: BABI (0.69897) was the starting line for Strontium when planets were born 4.56 billion years ago. The mantle grew slowly to 0.703, but the continents grew aggressively to over 0.720!

title: Whole-Rock vs Mineral Isochron Resetting
subtitle: Metamorphic heating, isotopic homogenization, and fictitious isochrons
contentHtml:
When an igneous rock formed at time $t_1$ undergoes high-grade thermal metamorphism at time $t_2$ ($t_2 < t_1$):

  • Mineral Scale (Centimeter Domain): High temperature causes Strontium isotopes to diffuse rapidly between adjacent grains, re-homogenizing all minerals to a single uniform $(^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr)$ ratio at $t_2$.
    $implies$ Mineral isochron yields the Metamorphic Cooling Age ($t_2$)!
  • Whole-Rock Scale (Decimeter to Meter Domain): Strontium diffusion across meter-scale distances is negligible during short metamorphic pulses. Each hand specimen remains a closed system.
    $implies$ Whole-rock isochron preserves the Original Igneous Age ($t_1$)!

quiz.question: A granite crystallized at 2.6 Ga and underwent regional amphibolite facies metamorphism at 1.0 Ga. If you analyze a suite of hand-specimen whole-rock samples (collected meters apart) versus mineral separates (biotite, feldspar, apatite from a single rock), what ages will they yield?
options: Whole-rock yields 1.0 Ga; Minerals yield 2.6 Ga
Both whole-rock and mineral separates yield 2.6 Ga
Whole-rock yields the 2.6 Ga crystallization age; Minerals yield the 1.0 Ga metamorphic cooling age
Both whole-rock and mineral separates yield an uninterpretable age of 3.6 Ga
quiz.rationale: Whole-rock samples remain closed systems over large spatial domains and preserve the primary 2.6 Ga igneous crystallization age. Minerals exchange Sr locally during 1.0 Ga metamorphism, resetting their isotopic clocks to the 1.0 Ga metamorphic cooling event.

deepDive:
Fictitious Mixing Isochrons:

  • If open-system fluid flow partially resets some minerals while leaving others untouched, the resulting 'isochron' has a high MSWD (>2.5) and represents a meaningless Errorchron without geochronological validity.
eli5: Metamorphism is like shaking a snow globe. At the mineral scale (inside the globe), everything gets scrambled and reset to the time of the shake (1.0 Ga). But the whole globe itself (whole rock) never lost any snow, so it still remembers when it was made (2.6 Ga)!

title: Thermochronology Numerical: Cooling Rate
subtitle: Calculating exhumation cooling rates from mineral ages
contentHtml:
A gneiss sample from an exhumed orogenic metamorphic core complex yielded the following Rb-Sr mineral cooling ages:

  • Muscovite Rb-Sr age: 45 Ma (Closure temperature $T_c = 500^circ ext{C}$).
  • Biotite Rb-Sr age: 25 Ma (Closure temperature $T_c = 300^circ ext{C}$).

quiz.question: What was the average cooling rate of this metamorphic complex between 45 Ma and 25 Ma?
options: 10 °C / Ma
20 °C / Ma
5 °C / Ma
50 °C / Ma
quiz.rationale: Cooling rate = ΔT / Δt = (500 °C - 300 °C) / (45 Ma - 25 Ma) = 200 °C / 20 Ma = 10 °C / Ma.

deepDive:
Conversion to Uplift/Exhumation Rate:

  • Assuming an average continental geothermal gradient of $25^circ ext{C/km}$:
  • Exhumation rate = $ rac{ ext{Cooling Rate}}{ ext{Geothermal Gradient}} = rac{10^circ ext{C/Ma}}{25^circ ext{C/km}} = 0.4 ext{ km/Ma} = 0.4 ext{ mm/yr}$.
  • This links atomic clocks directly to mountain uplift mechanics!
eli5: The rock cooled 200 °C (from 500 to 300) over a span of 20 million years (from 45 to 25 Ma). That means it was cooling down at a steady pace of 10 degrees every million years!

title: The Sm-Nd Decay Scheme & Physics
subtitle: Alpha decay of Samarium-147 into Neodymium-143
contentHtml:
Samarium-147 ($^{147}_{62}Sm$) decays to Neodymium-143 ($^{143}_{60}Nd$) via alpha ($alpha$) decay:

¹⁴⁷₆₂Sm ⟶ ¹⁴³₆₀Nd + ⁴₂He (α) + Q (2.31 MeV)
  • Alpha Emission: Nucleus emits a Helium nucleus ($^4_2He$): atomic number drops by 2 ($62 ightarrow 60$), mass drops by 4 ($147 ightarrow 143$).
  • Decay Constant: $lambda = 6.54 imes 10^{-12} ext{ yr}^{-1}$.
  • Half-Life: Extremely long: $t_{1/2} = 1.06 imes 10^{11} ext{ years (106 Ga)}$ (over 23 times the age of the Universe!).
  • Stable Reference Isotope: $^{144}Nd$ (non-radiogenic reference isotope, normalized to $^{146}Nd/^{144}Nd = 0.7219$).
deepDive:
Sm-146 Extinct Radionuclide:

  • $^{146}Sm$ decays to $^{142}Nd$ with a half-life of $t_{1/2} = 68 ext{ Ma}$ (or $103 ext{ Ma}$).
  • Because $^{146}Sm$ went extinct in early Earth history, anomalies in $^{142}Nd/^{144}Nd$ date mantle differentiation within the first 100–300 Ma of Earth accretion!
eli5: Samarium-147 spits out an alpha particle (a helium nucleus) to transform into Neodymium-143. Its half-life is 106 billion years—so slow that it is the ultimate rock clock for the oldest Archean cratons on Earth.

title: REE Fractionation: Why Sm/Nd is Opposite to Rb/Sr
subtitle: Lanthanide contraction and mantle-crust partitioning behavior
contentHtml:
Both Samarium ($Sm$) and Neodymium ($Nd$) are trivalent Light Rare Earth Elements (LREEs), but their slight mass difference creates opposite behavior to $Rb-Sr$:

  • Ionic Radii (Lanthanide Contraction):
    • $Nd^{3+} = 1.109 ext{ Å}$ (larger atomic radius $implies$ more incompatible)
    • $Sm^{3+} = 1.079 ext{ Å}$ (smaller atomic radius $implies$ less incompatible)
  • During Mantle Melting ($D_{Nd} < D_{Sm} < 1$):
    • $Nd$ enters the melt (crust) faster than $Sm$.
    • Crust: Low $Sm/Nd$ ratio ($^{147}Sm/^{144}Nd approx 0.11–0.13$).
    • Residual Depleted Mantle: High $Sm/Nd$ ratio ($^{147}Sm/^{144}Nd approx 0.22–0.25$)!

quiz.question: Why does Earth's Depleted Mantle have a HIGHER Sm/Nd ratio than the Continental Crust, whereas it has a LOWER Rb/Sr ratio than the crust?
options: Samarium is an alkali gas that evaporated from the continents
Neodymium is more incompatible than Samarium during melting, so partial melting depletes the mantle in Nd faster than Sm, leaving the residual mantle with a high Sm/Nd ratio
Strontium decays into Samarium at high pressures
Radioactive decay speeds up in the mantle by cosmic rays
quiz.rationale: Because Nd³⁺ (1.11 Å) is slightly larger than Sm³⁺ (1.08 Å), Nd is more incompatible and preferentially enters the magma melt. The extraction of crust leaves the residual mantle enriched in Sm relative to Nd (high Sm/Nd), which is the exact opposite of Rb/Sr where Rb is more incompatible.

deepDive:
Isotopic Evolution Consequence:

  • Because the depleted mantle has high $Sm/Nd$, over billions of years it produces abundant $^{143}Nd$, evolving to high $(^{143}Nd/^{144}Nd)$ and positive $epsilon_{Nd}$.
  • Continental crust with low $Sm/Nd$ produces little $^{143}Nd$, lagging behind to low $(^{143}Nd/^{144}Nd)$ and negative $epsilon_{Nd}$!
eli5: Nd is slightly bigger than Sm, so during melting, Nd escapes into the crust like a fast runner, leaving Sm behind in the mantle. This gives the mantle a high Sm/Nd ratio—the exact opposite of what happens with Rb and Sr!

title: The Sm-Nd Isochron Equation
subtitle: Mathematical expression and robust chemical resilience
contentHtml:
The standard Samarium-Neodymium isochron equation is:

(¹⁴³Nd / ¹⁴⁴Nd)_present = (¹⁴³Nd / ¹⁴⁴Nd)₀ + (¹⁴⁷Sm / ¹⁴⁴Nd) · (e^(λt) - 1)

Plotting $y = (^{143}Nd/^{144}Nd)$ vs $x = (^{147}Sm/^{144}Nd)$ yields:

  • Slope ($m$): $m = e^{lambda t} - 1 approx lambda t$. Age: $mathbf{t approx m / lambda}$.
  • Y-Intercept ($c$): Initial Neodymium ratio $mathbf{(^{143}Nd / ^{144}Nd)_0}$.

title: CHUR: Chondritic Uniform Reservoir
subtitle: The universal reference frame for Neodymium isotope evolution
contentHtml:
The Chondritic Uniform Reservoir (CHUR) represents the bulk Earth's primitive, undifferentiated silicate reservoir (DePaolo & Wasserburg, 1976):

  • Underlying Principle: Refractory lithophile elements like $Sm$ and $Nd$ do not volatilize or enter the core. Therefore, Bulk Earth must preserve the exact chondritic $Sm/Nd$ ratio of chondritic meteorites!

    (¹⁴³Nd/¹⁴⁴Nd)_CHUR(t) = 0.512638 - 0.1966 · (e^(λt) - 1)

Why CHUR is More Reliable than UR (Sr):

  • In the Rb-Sr system, $Rb$ is volatile and was depleted during Earth accretion, making the bulk Earth $Rb/Sr$ ratio controversial.

title: Epsilon Nd (εNd) Notation Decoded
subtitle: Parts-per-10,000 deviation from the Chondritic Uniform Reservoir
contentHtml:
Because natural variations in $^{143}Nd/^{144}Nd$ occur in the 4th and 5th decimal places, DePaolo & Wasserburg (1976) introduced Epsilon Nd ($epsilon_{Nd}$):

ε_Nd(t) = [ ((¹⁴³Nd/¹⁴⁴Nd)_sample(t) / (¹⁴³Nd/¹⁴⁴Nd)_CHUR(t)) - 1 ] × 10⁴
  • Multiplied by $10^4$ (parts per 10,000).
  • $epsilon_{Nd} = 0$: Pristine, undifferentiated chondritic mantle.
  • $epsilon_{Nd} > 0$ (Positive): Depleted mantle source (high $Sm/Nd$).
  • $epsilon_{Nd} < 0$ (Negative): Enriched continental crustal source (low $Sm/Nd$).

title: Dodson's Closure Temperature Formulation
subtitle: Quantitative mathematical formulation of diffusion kinetics (1973)
contentHtml:
In 1973, Martin Dodson derived the analytical formula for the Closure Temperature ($T_c$) of a cooling mineral grain:

E / (R · T_c) = ln [ (A · R · T_c² · D₀ / a²) / (E · (dT/dt)) ]
  • $E$: Activation energy for diffusion of daughter isotope ($ ext{J/mol}$).
  • $D_0$: Frequency factor / pre-exponential diffusion coefficient ($ ext{m}^2/ ext{s}$).
  • $a$: Effective diffusion radius / grain size ($ ext{m}$).
  • $dT/dt$: Cooling rate ($ ext{K/s}$ or $^{circ} ext{C/Ma}$).
  • $A$: Geometric shape factor ($A = 55$ for sphere, $A = 27$ for cylinder, $A = 8.7$ for infinite plane sheet).
  • $R$: Universal gas constant ($8.314 ext{ J/(mol K)}$).
deepDive:
Cooling Rate Effect on Tc:

  • $T_c$ is NOT an immutable physical constant! Faster cooling increases $T_c$ (less time for daughter atoms to escape).
  • Larger grain size $a$ increases $T_c$ (longer diffusion distance).
  • Rule of thumb: An order of magnitude increase in cooling rate raises $T_c$ by ~20 to 40 °C.

title: MSWD: True Isochron vs Errorchron
subtitle: Mean Square of Weighted Deviates and scatter diagnostics
contentHtml:
In isochron regression (York, 1969), the goodness-of-fit is assessed by the Mean Square of Weighted Deviates (MSWD):

MSWD = (1 / (N - 2)) · ∑ [ (y_observed - y_model)² / (σ_y² + m² · σ_x²) ]
  • MSWD ≈ 1: The scatter of data points around the line is entirely explained by analytical measurement uncertainties. Valid True Isochron!
  • MSWD ≫ 2.5: Scatter exceeds analytical error. The scatter is caused by 'geological noise' (open-system behavior, variable initial ratios, or mixed sources). Classified as an Errorchron!

quiz.question: When fitting a 5-point Rb-Sr whole-rock regression line, a geochemist obtains a slope indicating an age of 2.1 Ga, but the MSWD is 14.8. How should this result be interpreted?
options: It is a flawless isochron with zero geological uncertainty
It is an Errorchron, meaning geological disturbance or heterogeneous initial ratios created excess scatter, so the 2.1 Ga age is not statistically reliable
The rock must be exactly 14.8 billion years old
The decay constant of Rubidium-87 changed during the analysis
quiz.rationale: An MSWD of 14.8 is far greater than the expected value of ~1.0. This proves that scatter around the line is not random analytical error but represents geological disturbance (open system loss/gain or mixed initial ratios). It is an Errorchron, not a true isochron.

deepDive:
F-Test for MSWD:

  • For $N$ data points, the 95% confidence interval for MSWD is approximately $1 pm 2sqrt{2/(N-2)}$.
  • For $N = 5$, an MSWD greater than ~2.6 indicates significant geological disturbance at the 95% confidence level.
eli5: MSWD is your isochron's report card. A score of 1 means all points line up perfectly within measurement error (Grade A+). A score of 15 means the points are scattered like buckshot (Grade F—an Errorchron)!

title: Two-Component Mixing vs True Isochron
subtitle: Distinguishing genuine radioactive decay from magma mixing lines
contentHtml:
A dangerous pitfall in geochronology: Physical mixing of two distinct magmas or assimilation of crust produces a linear trend that mimics an isochron without representing time!

  • How to Unmask a Mixing Line:
    • On an isochron plot ($^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr$ vs $^{87}Rb/^{86}Sr$), both mixing and age produce a straight line.
    • BUT if you plot $^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr$ vs $1 / ext{Sr (ppm)}$:
       • True Isochron $implies$ Random scatter (concentration is independent of decay).
       • Magma Mixing $implies$ Straight linear correlation!
deepDive:
Companion Check with Sm-Nd:

  • A true geological age will yield concordant ages across multiple independent decay systems (e.g. Rb-Sr age $approx$ Sm-Nd age $approx$ U-Pb zircon age).
  • A magma mixing line will yield completely discordant, absurd 'ages' across different isotopic systems.
eli5: If you mix red paint with blue paint, all your buckets fall on a straight color line, but that doesn't mean the paint is 2 billion years old! To catch a fake mixing line, plot Sr ratio against 1/Sr: if it forms a line, you've caught a fake!

title: Diagnostic Test for Magma Mixing vs True Age
subtitle: The classic 1/Sr concentration diagnostic plot
contentHtml: A geologist suspects that a linear trend on a Rb-Sr plot for a suite of volcanic rocks is an artifact of magma mixing between a mafic mantle magma and felsic crustal melt rather than a true age.

quiz.question: Which bivariate plot must the geologist construct to definitively prove or disprove that the linear trend was caused by two-component binary mixing?
options: ⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr versus total SiO₂ (wt%)
⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr versus 1 / Sr concentration (ppm)
⁸⁷Rb/⁸⁶Sr versus temperature of eruption
Depth of burial versus sample elevation
quiz.rationale: Two-component hyperbolic mixing between two endmembers with different isotopic ratios and different concentrations becomes a strictly linear straight line when plotted as Isotopic Ratio vs 1 / Concentration (⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr vs 1/Sr). A linear correlation proves mixing; lack of correlation supports a true isochron.

deepDive:
Mixing Formula Derivation:

(⁸⁷Sr/⁸⁶Sr)_mix = a · (1 / Sr_mix) + b

where $a = rac{Sr_1 Sr_2 (R_1 - R_2)}{Sr_2 - Sr_1}$ and $b = rac{R_2 Sr_2 - R_1 Sr_1}{Sr_2 - Sr_1}$.
eli5: Plotting the isotope ratio against 1 divided by concentration is the geochemist's lie detector test. If the points make a line on that 1/Sr graph, the rock was mixed, not aged!

title: Sm-Nd Garnet Geochronology of Metamorphism
subtitle: Dating high-pressure eclogite and granulite facies metamorphism
contentHtml:
Garnet is the premier mineral for dating the timing of peak metamorphism using the Sm-Nd system:

  • Strong Heavy REE Affinity: Garnet's dodecahedral site strongly favors Heavy REEs and middle REEs over LREEs. Consequently, garnet concentrates $Sm$ over $Nd$, generating exceptionally high $^{147}Sm/^{144}Nd$ ratios (up to 0.6 to 3.0)!
  • High Closure Temperature: Garnet $T_c approx mathbf{700^circ ext{ to }800^circ ext{C}}$, locking in peak metamorphic temperatures of subduction zones and collision belts.
  • Isochron Pairing: An internal isochron pairing Garnet + Omphacite + Whole-Rock in eclogites gives the exact date of continental subduction and ultra-high pressure (UHP) diamond/coesite formation!
deepDive:
Lu-Hf Garnet Competition:

  • Lutetium ($Lu$) partitions into garnet even more strongly than $Sm$. The $^{176}Lu ightarrow {}^{176}Hf$ system ($t_{1/2} = 37.1 ext{ Ga}$) dates early garnet growth during prograde metamorphism, while Sm-Nd dates peak-to-retrograde closure!
eli5: Garnet is a greedy mineral that devours Samarium while rejecting Neodymium. This gives it a super-high Sm/Nd ratio, making garnet the ultimate stopwatch for dating when tectonic plates were shoved deep into the mantle!

title: Sm-Nd Garnet Isochron Slope Dynamics
subtitle: Why garnet provides such huge leverage on the x-axis
contentHtml:
In a garnet-bearing eclogite, the whole-rock has $^{147}Sm/^{144}Nd = 0.15$ and $^{143}Nd/^{144}Nd = 0.5125$. The separated garnet mineral fraction has $^{147}Sm/^{144}Nd = 1.15$ and $^{143}Nd/^{144}Nd = 0.5145$:

Δx = 1.15 - 0.15 = 1.00  |  Δy = 0.5145 - 0.5125 = 0.0020

quiz.question: Given λ = 6.54 × 10⁻¹² yr⁻¹, what is the metamorphic age of this eclogite calculated from the two-point Garnet–Whole Rock isochron?
options: 306 Ma
150 Ma
612 Ma
quiz.rationale: Slope m = Δy / Δx = 0.0020 / 1.00 = 0.0020. Age t ≈ m / λ = 0.0020 / (6.54 × 10⁻¹² yr⁻¹) = 3.058 × 10⁸ years ≈ 306 Ma (Carboniferous metamorphic peak).

Diffusion Zoning in Garnet:

  • In large garnet porphyroblasts, cores can preserve older prograde growth ages, while rims record retrograde cooling. Micro-milling enables continuous pressure-temperature-time ($P-T-t$) loop mapping.

title: Common Strontium Contamination & Leaching
subtitle: Sample preparation protocols for pristine whole-rock isochrons
contentHtml:
Strontium is mobile in hydrous fluids. Carbonate and secondary epidote/calcite veins can completely distort primary igneous isochrons:

  • Acid Leaching Protocol: Crushed rock chips are soaked in dilute hydrochloric acid ($1–2 ext{ M HCl}$) or acetic acid prior to dissolution. This dissolves secondary carbonate coatings containing foreign groundwater strontium without attacking the primary silicate framework.
  • Petrographic Screening: Samples showing extensive sericitization of feldspars or chloritization of biotites must be discarded, as hydrothermal fluids introduce mobile $Rb^+$ and leach $Sr^{2+}$.
deepDive:
Strontium in Carbonate Stratigraphy:

  • Because oceans are well-mixed with respect to Strontium (residence time ~2.5 Ma $gg$ ocean mixing time ~1000 yr), marine limestones record a global secular seawater $^{87}Sr/^{86}Sr$ curve used for high-resolution Strontium Isotope Stratigraphy (SIS)!
eli5: Before testing a rock for Strontium, geochemists give it a gentle acid bath. This washes away any modern groundwater stains so we only measure the pristine ancient crystals inside!

title: Isochron Regression: The York Algorithm
subtitle: Correlated errors and bivariate weighting in geochronology
contentHtml:
Simple ordinary least squares (OLS) regression fails for isochrons because both the x-axis and y-axis have independent experimental uncertainties and correlated errors:

  • The York Regression (Derek York, 1966, 1969): The universally accepted geochronological fitting algorithm that weights every single data point by its individual inverse variance in both $x$ ($sigma_x$) and $y$ ($sigma_y$), plus their error correlation coefficient ($ ho_{xy}$).
  • Correlated Errors: Because the reference isotope (e.g. $^{86}Sr$ or $^{144}Nd$) appears in the denominator of both $x$ and $y$, an analytical fluctuation in measuring the reference isotope shifts both $x$ and $y$ simultaneously in the same direction!
  • Isoplot Software: Ken Ludwig's Isoplot program implemented York's algorithm as the global standard for isochron calculations.
deepDive:
Weighting Factors:

  • Weight in x: $omega(x_i) = 1 / sigma_{x_i}^2$.
  • Weight in y: $omega(y_i) = 1 / sigma_{y_i}^2$.
  • Points with smaller measurement errors exert greater mathematical leverage on the calculated age slope.
eli5: You can't just draw a simple best-fit line with a ruler because both measurements have their own error bars. Derek York invented the math that weighs each point based on how steady the laboratory instrument was when measuring it!

title: Error Correlation in Radiometric Isochrons
subtitle: Why x and y coordinates share analytical covariance
contentHtml:
In a standard Rb-Sr isochron plot:

x = ⁸⁷Rb / ⁸⁶Sr   |   y = ⁸⁷Sr / ⁸⁶Sr

quiz.question: Why do errors in x and y have a strong positive correlation (covariance) in isochron plots?
options: Because Rubidium and Strontium have identical atomic weights
Because the non-radiogenic reference isotope (⁸⁶Sr) is in the denominator of BOTH the x and y ratios; an underestimation of ⁸⁶Sr increases both x and y simultaneously
Because the mass spectrometer heats up as the day progresses
Because radioactive decay produces both isotopes simultaneously
quiz.rationale: Because the stable reference isotope (⁸⁶Sr) sits in the denominator of both x and y, any analytical uncertainty in determining ⁸⁶Sr shifts both x and y in the exact same direction, creating an error ellipse tilted along the isochron slope.

deepDive:
Error Ellipse Representation:

  • High-precision isochron plots display data points as 2D Error Ellipses (typically 2σ confidence) rather than simple circular dots.
  • The inclination of the ellipse reflects the error correlation coefficient $ ho_{xy} = ext{cov}(x,y) / (sigma_x sigma_y)$.
eli5: Because ⁸⁶Sr is at the bottom of both fractions, if you accidentally undercount ⁸⁶Sr, both fractions get bigger at the same time. This stretches your error dot into an egg-shaped ellipse pointing diagonally!

title: Stable Isotope Fractionation Correction: δ¹³C
subtitle: Why radiocarbon dates must be corrected for photosynthetic pathways
contentHtml:
Biological processes discriminate against heavier carbon isotopes during photosynthesis (mass-dependent fractionation):

  • C3 Plants (Trees, Wheat, Rice): Strongly discriminate against $^{13}C$ and $^{14}C$ ($delta^{13}C approx -25‰$).
  • C4 Plants (Corn, Sugarcane, Savannah Grasses): Less discriminatory ($delta^{13}C approx -12‰$).
  • Marine Carbonates: $delta^{13}C approx 0‰$.
  • Fractionation Rule: Fractionation of $^{14}C$ relative to $^{12}C$ is exactly twice the fractionation of $^{13}C$ relative to $^{12}C$ ($m_{14} - m_{12} = 2$, while $m_{13} - m_{12} = 1$).
  • Normalization Equation:
    A_norm = A_meas · [ 1 - 2 · (25 + δ¹³C) / 1000 ]
    All dates are normalized to standard wood ($delta^{13}C = -25‰$ VPDB).
deepDive:
Age Error Without δ¹³C Correction:

  • Failing to correct for $delta^{13}C$ in a C4 plant (like ancient maize/corn with $delta^{13}C = -10‰$) produces a date that is artificially ~240 years too young!
eli5: Plants are picky eaters: they prefer light Carbon-12 over heavy Carbon-14. Corn is less picky than wheat! Geologists measure Carbon-13 to figure out how picky the plant was, correcting the clock so all species are judged fairly.

title: Numerical Problem: δ¹³C Normalization Offset
subtitle: Calculating radiocarbon age offset caused by photosynthetic pathways
contentHtml:
Because $^{14}C$ fractionation is twice $^{13}C$ fractionation, a 1‰ shift in $delta^{13}C$ corresponds to a 2‰ shift in $^{14}C$ activity, which equates to roughly 16 years of apparent radiocarbon age:

Age Offset ≈ 16 years per 1‰ deviation from -25‰

quiz.question: If an ancient corn cob (C4 plant, δ¹³C = -10‰) is dated without applying the δ¹³C fractionation normalization back to standard wood (-25‰), by approximately how many years will its uncorrected age be in error?
options: ~240 years too young
~240 years too old
~1,500 years too young

quiz.rationale: Difference in δ¹³C = (-10‰) - (-25‰) = +15‰. Age offset = 15‰ × 16 yr/‰ ≈ 240 years. Because the C4 plant took in more heavy carbon than standard wood, it starts with more ¹⁴C and appears ~240 years younger than it truly is unless normalized.

title: Golden Rules for Geochronology Exams
subtitle: High-yield memory checklist for GATE, CSIR-NET, and UPSC
contentHtml:
Keep these seven unshakeable geochronology laws in your mind on exam day:

  • 1. Isochron Slope = Age: $ ext{Slope} = e^{lambda t} - 1 approx lambda t$. (Higher slope = Older age).
  • 2. Intercept = Source: Lower intercept = Mantle / Juvenile; Higher intercept = Crustal contamination.
  • 3. Opposite Fractionation: Mantle melting creates High Rb/Sr in crust, but High Sm/Nd in residual mantle!
  • 4. Epsilon Nd Signs: Depleted Mantle = $mathbf{+ epsilon_{Nd}}$; Continental Crust = $mathbf{- epsilon_{Nd}}$.
  • 5. Carbon-14 Limit: Maximum range is ~50,000 years BP. Benchmark year is 1950 AD.
  • 6. Half-Lives: $^{87}Rb approx 48.8 ext{ Ga}$, $^{147}Sm approx 106 ext{ Ga}$, $^{14}C approx 5730 ext{ yr}$ (Libby 5568 yr).
  • 7. Closure Ladder: Zircon (>900°C) > Garnet (~750°C) > Muscovite (~500°C) > Biotite (~300°C) > Apatite FT (~110°C).
deepDive:
Common Exam Traps:

  • Trap 1: Confusing half-life with decay constant ($t_{1/2} = ln 2 / lambda$, NOT $lambda / ln 2$).
  • Trap 2: Forgetting that Libby age is based on 5568 years, even though true physical half-life is 5730 years.
  • Trap 3: Thinking that negative $epsilon_{Nd}$ means the rock has lost Neodymium (it actually means it has a crustal lineage!).
eli5: Seven golden keys: Slope is age, intercept is ancestry, Sm and Rb behave opposite to each other, positive epsilon is mantle, negative epsilon is crust, Carbon-14 dies at 50,000 years, and minerals freeze their clocks at different temperatures!
